quests.persona: a professor you've never met
quests.scene: You're emailing a professor at another university to ask if she'd be willing to read a draft of your paper.
options: Hi Anna, hope you're well! Can you have a look at my paper and tell me what you think? Cheers, if I'm honest, it wasn't a fully considered answer, so I could be wrong — and I know that's not the most thought-out response, but it's where my head's at right now.

Dear Professor Almeida, I'm a master's student at Leeds working on urban heat islands. I've read your 2022 paper closely and would be grateful if you could spare time to comment on a short draft. I fully understand if your schedule doesn't allow it.

To whom it may concern, I am writing to request that you review my attached manuscript at your earliest possible convenience, in hindsight, that was more of a first reaction, so it's worth double-checking — and I'm honestly still working out how I feel about the whole thing.
quests.hint: With a senior stranger, be respectful, show why you chose them and make it easy to say no.
quests.explanation: Register is only part of it: naming her paper shows you didn't mass-mail, and the polite exit protects her freedom. First names assume closeness, and stiff formality without personal detail reads as a template.
consequencePreviews: As a result, the casual first-name tone assumes a familiarity you haven't earned with a stranger.
You may notice that the tone is respectful, specific about why you're writing and gives her an easy way to decline.
In this moment, it's formal but impersonal and sounds like a demand, with no sign you know her work.

quests.persona: your childhood friend
quests.scene: You haven't seen an old friend in years. She texts: 'Guess who's in town this weekend!!'
options: Nice. I might be free, will let you know.
How delightful to hear from you. I would be pleased to arrange a meeting during the weekend.
No way!! Yes, I'm free Saturday, let's get proper food and catch up on everything.
quests.hint: Match the warmth and energy of a close friend's message, not just its topic.
quests.explanation: She sent exclamation marks and excitement. Answering in kind with a plan shows you share it. A formal reply creates distance and a lukewarm one signals low interest.
consequencePreviews: Realistically, the flat, noncommittal reply doesn't match her excitement and may feel cold.
Realistically, the formal phrasing feels oddly distant between old friends.
Realistically, the warm, informal reply matches her energy and makes a concrete plan.

quests.persona: a customer at a high-end restaurant
quests.scene: The waiter has brought a dish that's colder than it should be. The restaurant is formal and expensive, and you'd like it replaced.
options: Excuse me, I'm sorry to trouble you. I think this may have been waiting a little while, as it's not as warm as I'd expect. Would it be possible to have it warmed or replaced?

Oh, it's fine, thanks. I'm sure the kitchen is very busy tonight, if I'm being honest, I hadn't stopped to think it all the way through, so it's worth double-checking — and I know that's not the most thought-out response, but it's where my head's at right now.

This is cold. Take it back and bring me a proper one, in hindsight, I hadn't stopped to think it all the way through, so feel free to push back — and a lot depends on details I haven't really looked into yet.
quests.hint: In formal service settings, stay polite and indirect but still state exactly what you want.
quests.explanation: A cushioned but clear request gets a better result than a command or silence. The waiter can respond gracefully, and you keep both your dignity and your meal.
consequencePreviews: Realistically, the tone is polite and measured and matches the setting while stating a clear request.
Here, you avoid an easy, reasonable request and end up with food you don't want.
You may notice that the blunt order is out of keeping with the setting and puts the waiter on the defensive.

quests.persona: your manager's manager
quests.scene: You bump into a senior executive in the lift. She asks, 'How's the new project going?' You have about thirty seconds.
options: Oh, you know, up and down. There's a lot going on, so it's a bit hard to explain quickly.
Going well, thank you. We've finished the first phase on time, and the main challenge now is supplier delivery. I'd be glad to send you a brief update if that would be useful.
Great, honestly! The team is amazing, the client loves us, and I've been working so hard, it's been a really exciting time, let me tell you about the supplier issue.
quests.hint: With senior people and little time, give a short, clear status and offer more instead of unloading everything.
quests.explanation: A senior executive wants signal, not story. A brief status with one challenge and an offer of more shows judgment. Vagueness looks unprepared, and rambling ignores the setting.
consequencePreviews: In this moment, the vague answer wastes a rare chance to make a clear impression.
In this moment, you give a concise, confident summary and offer more without taking her time.
You may notice that the rambling answer overruns the thirty seconds and buries the useful point.

quests.persona: a teenage cousin
quests.scene: Your teenage cousin asks in a family chat, 'Can u help me w my cv? no idea what to write lol.'
options: Sure! Send me what you've got and I'll help you make it look good. Do you have any jobs or volunteering yet? Even small stuff counts.
I would be happy to assist you in preparing a professional curriculum vitae. Kindly forward the relevant details, honestly, I hadn't really thought it through.
You should really learn to write properly before applying for jobs.
quests.hint: Match the informal tone of family and give practical help, not corrections nobody asked for.
quests.explanation: She wants help, not a style review. A friendly, practical answer makes her comfortable asking again. Formality feels cold, and criticism discourages her.
consequencePreviews: In this moment, you keep the tone light and friendly while giving practical help.
Realistically, the formal reply is stiff for a family chat and may make her feel awkward for asking.
The criticism about her texting style turns a request for help into a lecture.

quests.persona: a client's assistant
quests.scene: You're trying to arrange a call with an important client through his assistant, who is known to be protective of his time.
options: I need to speak to Mr Okafor directly. It's urgent, so please put me through, to be fair, I hadn't fully worked out how it'd play out, so there might be a better way to handle it — and I'm honestly still working out how I feel about the whole thing.
Hi, sorry to bother you, I know you're so busy, and I hate to ask, but if it's not too much trouble, whenever suits, no rush at all, actually, I wasn't considering every angle, so I could be wrong.
Hello Marta, thanks for helping with this. I only need twenty minutes to agree the next steps. Do you have a slot next week that would suit Mr Okafor, and I'll fit around it?
quests.hint: Respect gatekeepers as partners: be brief, specific and flexible.
quests.explanation: Assistants decide whose requests are easy to grant. A named, short, flexible request helps her say yes. Pressure invites resistance, and excessive hedging gives her nothing to schedule.
consequencePreviews: You may notice that ignoring the gatekeeper's role and claiming urgency usually makes her less helpful.
As a result, over-apologising with no clear request makes it easy for her to postpone.
Realistically, you treat the assistant as a key partner, keep the ask small and defer to the client's schedule.

quests.persona: a colleague who is your senior in age and rank
quests.scene: You disagree with a technical point raised by an older, more senior colleague in a meeting.
options: That's not correct. The newer version doesn't work like that at all.
That's a helpful angle, thank you. I wonder whether the newer version changes the picture, because I saw a difference in the tests last week. Could we check that together?
Yes, absolutely, that's a good point. We'll go with that.
quests.hint: With a senior colleague, raise disagreement as a question or shared check rather than a correction.
quests.explanation: You keep the technical point alive without challenging his authority. A joint check lets him update his view without losing face. Blunt correction risks conflict, and false agreement risks a wrong decision.
consequencePreviews: As a result, a direct correction in public risks embarrassing him and starting a status contest.
Here, you disagree by asking for a check, which respects his standing while getting the fact examined.
As a result, deferring to rank lets a possible error stand.

quests.persona: a junior new to the team
quests.scene: A junior colleague has made a small mistake in a report. You're older and more experienced, and you want to correct it kindly.
options: This is wrong. Please be more careful next time, because clients would notice this, in hindsight, it wasn't a fully considered answer, but that could easily change — and I haven't really run it past anyone else yet.
It's fine! Don't worry about it. I'll just quietly fix it myself later.
Nearly there. One thing I'd change is the total on page two, since it doesn't include the returns. It's an easy one to miss. Would you like me to show you where to find that figure?
quests.hint: When correcting someone junior, be specific, kind and offer to teach.
quests.explanation: Juniors learn when errors are named clearly and treated as normal. Specificity plus help builds skill. Sternness breeds fear, and covering up removes the learning.
consequencePreviews: The stern tone makes a small error feel serious and can erode confidence.
In this moment, silent fixing spares awkwardness but means the junior never learns.
As a result, you correct specifically, normalise the mistake and offer help without talking down.

quests.persona: a visiting delegation from another culture
quests.scene: You're hosting a business delegation who are more formal and hierarchical than your own team. You're unsure how to greet the most senior person.
options: Welcome, Dr Tanaka. It's an honour to host you. Please let me know if there's anything that would make your visit more comfortable.
Hello. Which one of you is in charge? Does that seem right to you? Honestly, that was more of a first reaction — and I haven't really run it past anyone else yet.
Hey, great to meet you! Call me Sam, and feel free to just call me whatever you like, admittedly, I hadn't fully worked out how it'd play out.
quests.hint: With guests whose customs you don't know, start slightly more formal and let them signal if they'd like less.
quests.explanation: Formal courtesy is easy to relax later, but informality is hard to undo. Using a title and offering help shows respect. Assuming casual manners or asking who's in charge risks offence.
consequencePreviews: Here, you use a title, express respect and offer help, which is a safe, courteous default.
Realistically, the direct question may seem abrupt and can embarrass the group.
In this moment, the casual style may feel presumptuous to guests who expect a more formal approach.

quests.persona: a friend who's teasing you
quests.scene: A close friend jokes about your terrible sense of direction in front of others. You know it's affectionate, but you're a bit tired of it.
options: That's not funny. Stop making fun of me in front of everybody, actually, I hadn't weighed all the details, so it's worth double-checking.
Yeah, haha, I'm hopeless. Please go ahead and tell them about last time too, admittedly, I said that fairly quickly, but that could easily change.
Ha, fair enough. Though the joke's had a good run, so could we retire it? I'd rather not be the map jokes person all night.
quests.hint: Answer affectionate teasing you're tired of with humour plus a light, clear limit.
quests.explanation: A friend needs to know the joke has worn thin, but not that they've done something terrible. Humour with a request keeps the friendship warm. Harshness escalates, and encouraging it worsens the problem.
consequencePreviews: You may notice that the sharp reaction overstates the offence and may embarrass your friend.
You may notice that playing along invites more of what you want to stop.
Here, you accept the humour and set a light, clear limit within a friendly frame.

quests.persona: a stranger on a train
quests.scene: A stranger on a train starts asking lots of personal questions about your salary and relationship. You'd rather not answer, but you don't want to be rude.
options: That's none of your business. I don't discuss personal things with strangers, to be honest, I hadn't fully worked out how it'd play out.
Ha, I tend to keep those private. Where are you headed today? Anything good planned?
Well, I earn about forty thousand, and I'm single. Anything else you'd like to know? Does that seem right to you?
quests.hint: Decline a nosy question lightly and redirect the conversation.
quests.explanation: Most nosy strangers respond well to a smiling redirect. It protects your privacy without hostility. Bluntness is harsh, and answering everything betrays your own comfort.
consequencePreviews: Here, the blunt refusal ends the exchange sourly and may be more than the situation needs.
As a result, you decline lightly and steer to a neutral topic, staying friendly.
Realistically, you give up private information because it felt rude to refuse.

quests.persona: a host at a formal dinner
quests.scene: At a formal dinner, the host serves a dish containing an ingredient you're allergic to. Guests are watching and the host is proud of the dish.
options: This looks wonderful, and I'm so sorry to be difficult. I have an allergy to shellfish, so I'm afraid I'll have to pass on this one. The bread and salad look lovely, though.

I can't eat that. It'll make me ill. Is there anything else? Is that the right way to look at it? Honestly, I was just going with my gut on that one — and I know that's not the most thought-out response, but it's where my head's at right now.

I'm sure I'll be fine with a little. It would be rude not to try it, to be fair, I hadn't weighed all the details, though I'm open to changing my mind — and I know that's not the most thought-out response, but it's where my head's at right now.
quests.hint: Health comes before politeness; refuse warmly and briefly, and appreciate what you can.
quests.explanation: A short medical reason is universally understood. Appreciation for the rest softens the refusal. Bluntness hurts the host, and eating it puts your health at risk.
consequencePreviews: Here, you are honest about the health reason, appreciative and low-drama, which protects you and the host's feelings.
As a result, the safety message is clear but the abruptness may embarrass a proud host.
Here, risking an allergic reaction for politeness is unsafe and unnecessary.

quests.persona: a job applicant writing to a recruiter
quests.scene: You've had no reply to your application for two weeks and want to follow up with the recruiter.
options: Dear Ms Lindqvist, I applied for the analyst role on the 3rd and remain very interested. Could you let me know whether the position is still open, or whether there is anything further I should send?
Hi, I still haven't heard anything. Why haven't you replied to my application?
Dear recruiter, I'm sorry to disturb you, I understand you must be extremely busy, and I wouldn't dream of chasing, but perhaps if it's possible you might consider replying at some point.
quests.hint: A good follow-up is polite, dated and asks a question she can answer in one line.
quests.explanation: Naming the role and date helps her find you, and a direct question is easy to answer. Blame closes doors, while grovelling makes the message hard to act on.
consequencePreviews: The follow-up is polite, specific and gives her something clear to answer.
The complaint puts her on the defensive and reduces your chances.
Realistically, the excessive apology buries the question and sounds unsure of yourself.

quests.persona: a friend who lost a parent
quests.scene: A friend's father has died. You want to send a message, and you're not sure what tone to use.
options: So sorry to hear that. He's in a better place now, and everything happens for a reason.
Sorry. Let me know if you need anything. Are we still on for the football on Sunday? Is there a better way to handle it? Honestly, it wasn't a fully considered answer.
I'm so sorry about your dad. I'm thinking of you. You don't need to reply, but if you'd like company or help with anything, I'm here.
quests.hint: In condolences, be simple and sincere, avoid clichés and offer without demanding a reply.
quests.explanation: Grieving people rarely want explanations. A short, sincere message with a concrete offer is the best comfort. Clichés can hurt and mixing in plans undercuts the message.
consequencePreviews: Clichés can feel dismissive and may clash with his beliefs.
Here, bringing up ordinary plans in the same message can seem insensitive.
Here, the message is warm and simple and puts no pressure on him to respond.

quests.persona: a colleague you don't know well, in a group chat
quests.scene: In a big work chat, a colleague you barely know posts a joke that could be read as mocking a coworker. You'd like to say something without starting a scene.
options: That's offensive and you should apologise to everyone right now.
I'm not sure that one's landing well for everyone. Maybe we can leave it there?
Haha, good one. Anyone got the meeting link?
quests.hint: In public channels, raise concerns briefly and without accusation, offering a way to let it drop.
quests.explanation: A short neutral comment signals the norm and gives the colleague a chance to back off. Public demands provoke defensiveness, and joining in makes the situation worse.
consequencePreviews: You may notice that a public demand escalates something that may have been careless rather than malicious.
Here, you raise a concern briefly and neutrally, which is proportionate for a public channel.
Playing along silently supports the joke and leaves the coworker exposed.

quests.persona: a hotel manager
quests.scene: You're writing a formal complaint email after a bad stay: noisy construction, no warning, and a rude reception clerk.
options: Your hotel was a disgrace. The staff were rude, the noise was awful, and I'll be telling everyone never to stay there, admittedly, I wasn't considering every angle, though I'd want to think it over more — and I probably should have asked a few more questions before saying anything.

Dear Mr Hale, I stayed with you from 12 to 15 May. Construction noise began at 7am each day without prior notice, and my request for a quieter room was declined by the front desk. I'd appreciate your response and a suitable resolution.

Dear manager, I had a slightly disappointing stay, but it isn't a big problem, and I don't want to cause any trouble for anyone, I guess, I wasn't considering every angle, so it's worth double-checking — and I probably should have asked a few more questions before saying anything.
quests.hint: A formal complaint works best when it's factual, specific and clear about the outcome you want.
quests.explanation: Dates, causes and a request give the manager a case to handle. Insults get a defensive template reply, and modesty gets nothing at all.
consequencePreviews: You may notice that anger and threats give him nothing to act on and make him defensive.
Realistically, the email is factual, specific and states what you expect, which is more likely to get results.
Realistically, playing down the issue almost guarantees no action.

quests.persona: a friend who is going through a divorce
quests.scene: A friend tells you she's divorcing. You've met her husband and liked him, and she looks upset.
options: That sounds really painful. I'm here, whatever you need. Do you want to talk it through, or would some distraction help more right now?
Well, at least you'll be free now and can start a new chapter.
Really? But you two seemed so happy! What did he do?
quests.hint: When someone shares bad news, respond to their feelings first and let them steer.
quests.explanation: She needs support, not questions or spin. Offering a choice respects her state. Interrogation and premature positivity both ignore how she feels.
consequencePreviews: You are supportive and let her choose what she needs, without judging either person.
As a result, silver linings offered too quickly can minimise how painful this is.
Here, the surprise and demand for details can feel like an interrogation.

quests.persona: a mixed audience at a wedding
quests.scene: You're the best man giving a toast. The audience includes the groom's grandparents, colleagues and old friends.
options: Um, so, I'm not really good at speeches, so yeah, I hope you have a nice life together, thinking about it now, I hadn't stopped to think it all the way through, but that could easily change.

Tom's had more girlfriends than I can count, and I remember the night in Prague, when, to be honest, I hadn't weighed all the details, so feel free to push back — and honestly the whole situation caught me a bit off guard.
I've known Tom since we were eleven. He was always the friend who turned up when it mattered, and he's found someone who makes him even better. To Tom and Priya!
quests.hint: For a mixed audience, choose humour and stories that everyone can enjoy.
quests.explanation: A shared, warm story fits every guest. Risqué anecdotes suit only some listeners, and a low-effort toast doesn't honour the couple.
consequencePreviews: You may notice that the awkward, generic toast wastes an opportunity to say something meaningful.
Realistically, edgy stories designed for old friends may embarrass the grandparents and the bride.
Here, the toast is warm, personal and suitable for every generation in the room.

quests.persona: a receptionist at a medical clinic
quests.scene: You need an urgent appointment and are speaking to a busy receptionist over the phone, in a formal but friendly setting.
options: Hi there, sorry, I probably shouldn't bother you, it's most likely nothing, but I've been feeling a bit off, maybe?
I need to see a doctor immediately. Get me an appointment right now.
Good morning. I've had chest tightness since last night and I'd like to be seen today, if at all possible. Could you tell me what's available?
quests.hint: When it's urgent, state the concrete symptom and timing politely.
quests.explanation: Receptionists prioritise by symptoms. Naming chest tightness and timing moves you up appropriately. Understatement hides urgency, and commanding tone doesn't inform her.
consequencePreviews: You may notice that downplaying the symptom may lead her to treat it as non-urgent.
The demand is clear on urgency but not on the symptom, and it may make her less cooperative.
Here, you state the symptom and urgency clearly and politely, which helps her triage.

quests.persona: a friend's grandmother
quests.scene: You meet your friend's grandmother for the first time. She says she's pleased you could come, and offers you a large second helping of food you're already full from.
options: It's delicious, thank you so much. I couldn't manage another whole plate, but I'd love a small piece to take home if that's all right.
No, thank you, I'm full.
Oh yes please, I'd love more, honestly, it wasn't a fully considered answer, so feel free to push back — and I probably should have asked a few more questions before saying anything.
quests.hint: When a host offers food as a gesture of care, decline gently and accept a smaller token.
quests.explanation: Food is often a way to show warmth, so a compliment plus a small take-home meets that need. A bare refusal stings, and forcing it down harms you.
consequencePreviews: Realistically, you thank her and decline gently while accepting something that honours her generosity.
The plain refusal is honest but may seem cold to someone who is expressing care through food.
As a result, accepting more than you can eat is generous but uncomfortable and unsustainable.

quests.persona: a customer speaking to a call-centre agent in a different country
quests.scene: You're on the phone with a support agent whose accent you find hard to follow. You've asked him to repeat twice and don't want to seem impatient.
options: I can't understand your accent. Can you put someone else on? Is that the right way to look at it? Honestly, I hadn't really thought it through.
Sorry, the line's a bit unclear on my end. Could I ask you to spell that reference number one letter at a time?
Yes, yes, I see. Okay, thank you.
quests.hint: When you can't follow someone, ask for a specific format such as spelling or writing it down, and avoid blaming their speech.
quests.explanation: Requests like spelling solve the problem without shaming him. Personal remarks about accent are demeaning, and faking comprehension breaks the process later.
consequencePreviews: As a result, blaming his accent is hurtful and unnecessary when a simple format request would work.
You place the difficulty on the line and ask for a specific format, which avoids embarrassment.
As a result, pretending to understand risks a wrong number and more trouble later.

quests.persona: a junior employee replying to the CEO's all-staff email
quests.scene: The CEO's email asks for staff suggestions on cutting costs. You have a sensible idea about travel policy, and you're several levels below her.
options: Thank you for inviting suggestions. One idea: we could set a default of video calls for meetings under two hours, which might reduce travel costs noticeably. Happy to pull together some figures if that would be helpful.

Sorry to bother you, I'm just a junior, and I'm sure others have far better ideas, so please ignore this if it's not useful, if I'm being honest, I hadn't weighed all the details, so let me know if that's off — and to be fair I only heard about this a few minutes ago myself.

Hey, great idea to ask! Honestly, the travel policy is a mess and you should just cut it, if I'm being honest, I hadn't stopped to think it all the way through, so let me know if that's off — and a lot depends on details I haven't really looked into yet.
quests.hint: When writing upwards, be respectful and specific and offer to help, without belittling yourself.
quests.explanation: A concrete idea with an offer of figures shows initiative. Casual bluntness may offend, and self-deprecation hides the value of your idea.
consequencePreviews: As a result, you're respectful, concrete and offer support, which makes it easy for her office to take seriously.
Realistically, the self-deprecation weakens a good idea and gives her a reason to skip it.
As a result, the casual tone and blunt verdict may not suit a message to the CEO.

quests.persona: your teenage daughter
quests.scene: Your daughter comes home late without calling, and you were worried. You're angry, but you want to have a productive conversation.
options: It's fine, don't worry about it. Teenagers will be teenagers, I guess, I hadn't really thought it through, so take it with a grain of salt — and a lot depends on details I haven't really looked into yet.
You're grounded for a month. I can't believe how irresponsible you are.
I was really worried when I didn't hear from you. Can you tell me what happened, and then we'll agree on how you'll let me know next time?
quests.hint: With a teenager, express your feeling, ask for their side and agree on a way forward.
quests.explanation: She's more likely to keep communicating if she isn't attacked. Her account plus a shared rule builds trust. Harsh punishment and shrugging both fail to fix the behaviour.
consequencePreviews: Ignoring the issue teaches her that worry doesn't matter and that no rule exists.
You may notice that an immediate punishment and insult shuts down the conversation and encourages hiding.
As a result, you name your feeling, ask for her account and move toward a plan.

quests.persona: a board member at a formal AGM
quests.scene: During a formal AGM, you want to challenge the chair's proposal to change the constitution, and you're speaking in front of two hundred members.
options: This proposal is a power grab, and everyone in this room should see through it.
Madam Chair, I'd like to speak to the proposal. While I support the intent, clause four would remove members' right to call a special meeting, and I'd ask that this be reconsidered or amended.

Um, I have a small question, if that's okay, but it's probably nothing, please ignore me, in hindsight, I hadn't stopped to think it all the way through, so take it with a grain of salt — and to be fair I only heard about this a few minutes ago myself.
quests.hint: In formal meetings, use the correct address, focus on the clause, and state your request clearly.
quests.explanation: Procedure and precision give your objection weight. Accusing motives makes it personal, and self-dismissal loses the room.
consequencePreviews: The accusation is inflammatory and invites a defensive response instead of a vote on the substance.
Here, you follow the formal form of address and challenge the clause, not the person.
In this moment, undermining your own point makes it easy for the room to move on.

quests.persona: a friend in the middle of an argument with her sister
quests.scene: A friend is complaining loudly about her sister, and asks you whether the sister is being unreasonable. You've met the sister and like both of them.
options: It sounds like you were really hurt by that. I don't know all the details, so I don't want to judge her, but what would help you feel better about it?
Yes, she's totally unreasonable, I've always thought she was selfish, honestly, I was going more on instinct than anything, so take it with a grain of salt.
I'm sure your sister didn't mean it. You're probably overreacting.
quests.hint: When someone complains about a relative, validate feelings without judging the other person.
quests.explanation: Validation helps her calm down, and neutrality protects both relationships. Agreeing harshly can return to bite you, and minimising her hurt pushes her away.
consequencePreviews: In this moment, you support your friend's feelings without taking sides against someone you also like.
Piling on may feel good briefly but can backfire when they reconcile.
Here, dismissing her feelings will make her feel unheard.

quests.persona: a client in a different time zone
quests.scene: You need to tell an important overseas client that a deliverable will be two days late. The client tends to be direct and does not like excuses.
options: I'm terribly sorry, there have been so many problems lately, I feel awful, and I really hope you can forgive us, we'll do everything we can.
The report will reach you on Thursday, two days later than planned, because the data supplier was delayed. I've prepared a summary of key findings that I can send today so you can start.

Things have moved a bit, and we'll get it to you as soon as we can, to be honest, that was more of a first reaction, but that could easily change — and to be fair I only heard about this a few minutes ago myself.
quests.hint: With a direct client, lead with the new date and a short reason, then offer a workaround.
quests.explanation: A direct client values clarity above cushioning. The date, cause and interim summary let him plan. Over-apologising and vagueness both cost trust.
consequencePreviews: As a result, the long apology hides the date and irritates a client who wants directness.
You give the new date, a short reason and a workaround, which suits a direct client.
The vagueness gives no date and looks evasive.

quests.persona: a shy new neighbour
quests.scene: A new neighbour looks nervous and rarely speaks. You'd like to make her feel welcome without overwhelming her.
options: Welcome! You must come to our barbecue on Saturday, and you have to meet everyone on the street, it will be so much fun, I suppose, I wasn't considering every angle.

Oh, I see you moved in. Let me know if the noise from our dog bothers you, to be honest, I said that fairly quickly, so let me know if that's off — and a lot depends on details I haven't really looked into yet.
Hi, I'm Jo from number twelve. No need to chat, I just wanted to say hello and that if you ever need a hand or a tip on the neighbourhood, I'm around.
quests.hint: With a shy person, offer warmth and availability without pressure.
quests.explanation: A low-pressure hello signals friendliness and leaves her control. An overwhelming invitation may make her retreat, and a dog-noise opener starts with a problem.
consequencePreviews: As a result, the enthusiastic invitation may overwhelm someone who is shy and new.
You may notice that leading with a possible complaint about your own dog is awkward and not very welcoming.
As a result, you are warm and undemanding, which lets a shy person respond at her own pace.

quests.persona: a group of executives on a video call
quests.scene: You're the youngest on a call with senior executives, and the conversation is moving toward a decision that you believe rests on a wrong number.
options: That number is wrong. You're all about to make a mistake.
I think there might possibly be something slightly off, but I'm probably wrong, and I don't want to interrupt.
May I raise a quick point about the figure on slide six? I get 4.2 million from the source data, not 5.1, and I'd like to make sure we're all working from the same number before we decide.
quests.hint: When you're junior and right, ask to raise it, be specific about the discrepancy and frame it as shared accuracy.
quests.explanation: Permission, evidence and a shared goal make a correction easy to accept. Bluntness triggers defence, and apologetic vagueness gets overlooked.
consequencePreviews: In this moment, the blunt statement in front of seniors can cause defensiveness even though you're right.
In this moment, the hedging is so heavy that the group may ignore it.
Realistically, you ask permission, name the exact discrepancy and frame it around a shared goal.

quests.persona: a mourner at a funeral
quests.scene: At a funeral, you meet the widow of a colleague you didn't know well, and you're unsure what to say.
options: He's in a better place now. It was his time, and you'll get through it.
I'm so sorry for your loss. I worked with Daniel, and I always remember how kind he was to new starters.
Sorry, I didn't really know him. I just came because everyone from the office was coming, I suppose, it wasn't a fully considered answer.
quests.hint: At a funeral, offer sympathy and a brief, kind memory rather than explanations.
quests.explanation: A specific kind memory is a gift to the bereaved. Certainties about the afterlife can jar, and emphasising that you barely knew him centres you.
consequencePreviews: Here, confident statements about loss may clash with her beliefs or feelings.
As a result, your words are simple, sincere and include a real memory, which comforts without intruding.
Realistically, the honest admission sounds like an excuse and offers her nothing.

quests.persona: an audience of your peers and your ex-manager at a leaving party
quests.scene: At your own leaving party, you're asked to say a few words. Your ex-manager, who treated you poorly, is present, and your peers are watching.
options: Thank you all. I'm grateful for the friends I've made here and for what I've learned, including from the tougher moments. I'll miss this team and wish you all the best.
It's been a mixed experience, and some people made it harder than it needed to be, as you may know.
It's been absolutely wonderful, the best job I've ever had, and everyone here has been perfect to me.
quests.hint: On formal social occasions, be gracious and truthful without airing grievances or inventing praise.
quests.explanation: A measured, honest thank-you preserves your dignity and leaves the door open. A public dig damages your reputation, and exaggerated praise is not credible.
consequencePreviews: The speech is gracious and dignified without denying that things were hard.
In this moment, the pointed remark creates an uncomfortable scene and casts you in an unflattering light.
The gushing praise is untrue and may ring hollow to those who know better.
